notice: Empirical stress prior from public aircraft ADS-B broadcasts. It does not describe drone receivers. No actor attribution. See caveats.

definitions.sample_filter: airborne, src_type adsb_icao (own transponder), inside the region box, with barometric altitude; duplicates of (icao24, ts) removed
definitions.quality_sample: a sample with its own NIC (not carried forward from an earlier message)
definitions.episode: maximal run of one aircraft's consecutive quality samples, all strongly degraded, neighbours at most 120 s apart, at least 2 samples; duration is last minus first sample time
definitions.baseline: quality samples (or intervals starting at samples) that are not strongly degraded
definitions.degraded_episode: quality samples inside an episode (intervals: starting at a sample inside an episode)
definitions.isolated_degraded: strongly degraded runs shorter than the episode minimum belong to neither class; counted in n

strata.note: enroute is the union of mid and high; strata overlap by construction

definitions.update_interval: seconds between consecutive position samples of one aircraft-day, up to 600 s; longer gaps and samples flagged as a new leg are excluded and counted; quantiles use 0.1 s bins below 30 s
definitions.dropout: share of intervals longer than 20 s and 60 s
definitions.episode_rate: episodes started per aircraft hour of observed quality-sample time (neighbours within the gap)
definitions.transitions: probability that the next quality sample is strongly degraded given the current one is degraded or nominal, within one aircraft and gap
definitions.intervals: boot_lo/boot_hi: percentile bootstrap over aircraft-days; wilson_*: ignores clustering, too narrow; poisson_exact_*: assumes independent episodes, too narrow

caveats.summary: These parameters come from public aircraft ADS-B broadcasts, mostly at cruise-type altitudes, over the Gulf. They describe how aircraft avionics report position quality and how often those reports pause during en-route interference. They do NOT describe a drone-scale receiver, low-altitude urban multipath, or a small antenna. Use them only as an illustrative stress prior for scenario testing, never as a measured model of a drone's GNSS behaviour, and never as a certification input.
points: Source: adsb.lol globe_history archives of volunteer receivers (ODbL 1.0). Coverage differs by place and time.
NIC and NACp are accuracy classes that an aircraft transmits about its own position, not measured position errors.
A low NIC or NACp can also come from old avionics, installation faults or ADS-B version differences, so a degraded episode is evidence of degraded reporting, not proof of interference.

Update intervals and dropouts mix three things: aircraft transmission behaviour, receiver coverage gaps, and the thinning applied by the archive. They are not the dropout behaviour of a drone receiver.

In the archive, update intervals rarely run much beyond the 20 second mark that the source itself uses to flag a gap in position, so the upper tail of the update interval and the 20 second dropout share reflect archive sampling as well as real gaps. Read them as properties of this data source, not of a receiver.

Counts of samples are not independent (one aircraft contributes many consecutive samples). Wilson intervals treat samples as independent and are therefore too narrow; the bootstrap intervals resample aircraft-days and are the ones to use.
Parameters are built from the listed days only, which are development days. They may not transfer to other days or seasons.
A block marked insufficient does not have enough aircraft-days or events to report an interval, and is not a statement of zero.
No attribution: the file says nothing about who or what caused any degradation.
not_for: claims about a specific drone, receiver or site
attributing interference to any state or actor
